[Nextflow](https://www.nextflow.io/) is a workflow language that enables scalable and portable scientific workflows. 

This section does not teach you how to code or use Nextflow workflows. To get started learning Nextflow, we recommend the following training:

**Introductory**
- [Nextflow training](https://training.nextflow.io/latest/)
- [Nextflow for the life sciences](https://zenodo.org/records/16791039)

**Intermediate**
- [Nextflow on HPC](https://zenodo.org/records/17694728)
- [Customising nf-core](https://zenodo.org/records/20453332)


Instead, this section will describe different methods of running Nextflow specifically for NCI Gadi HPC. 

## Key points

### Lack of internet access on compute nodes

Nextflow is designed to pull resources (e.g. databases, updated software container versions) on the fly. Gadi compute nodes lack internet access, so if you attempt to run a workflow where the requirements are not found locally, Nextflow will attempt to download them and your run will fail. For this reason, it is required to ensure you have pre-downloaded all software containers and inputs beforehand. If your workflow requires a lot of containers, running the download (for example using the `nf-core pipelines download` command if you are running an nf-core pipeline) on `copyq` is recommended.

### Ways to run

On Gadi, Nextflow can be run:

- On the 'copyq' job queue with a Gadi configuration file
- On the persistent session nodes with a Gadi configuration file
- Within a single PBS job (not recommended for complex workflows)

### Why use a Nextflow Gadi configuration file 

When using the `copyq` or persistent sessions method, a Gadi configuration file is required. This file instructs Nextflow to send each run of each process to the PBS Pro job scheduler, to be submitted as its own separate job, with the resources and queue type specified within the config.

Without the Gadi configuration file, the processes will be run using the compute available to the session. In the case of a `copyq` job, this is restricted to 1 CPU. On the persistent session nodes, these are available under a fair use policy, and should *not* be used to run intensive processes, similar to the login nodes. Using a Gadi config enables your Nextflow workflow to access the vast compute available on the whole cluster.

A Gadi configuration file at minimum contains the resource specifics needed to run any Nextflow workflow on Gadi. The config can be further customised to over-ride the resource defaults set by the workflow developers, for example changing the number of CPUs for a process to better match the hardware setup on Gadi. These details are covered in the two intermediate training workshops suggested above. 

An example Gadi configuration file is included below.

### Software

We recommend using singularity for software when running Nextflow on Gadi. Docker is not supported on Gadi, and local installations are not recommended as they eschew the portability and reproducibility that make Nextflow so well suited to scientific data analysis. 

The Gadi config file will instruct Nextflow to use singularity, and the workflow codebase will describe the singularity images. 

To ensure your workflow can run on Gadi, you need to:

1. Pre-download the software images
2. Include commands to load the latest modules for `nextflow` and `singularity` within your job script (if using `copyq` ) or within your session (if using persistent sessions)


### Walltime

When running a Nextflow workflow on Gadi, the `run` command must be active for the entire duration that processes are running. When using the `copyq`, this means that all processes must complete within the 10 hour walltime limit imposed by that queue. The individual processes are subject to the walltime limits of the queue that they are run on, for example 48 hours for the `normal` queue. Queue time is important here too: If your workflow runs a process that requests 8 hours on the `normal` queue but was queued for 3 hours, this has already exceeded the 10 hours that the head job could be running on the `copyq`. 

To overcome this limitation with using the `copyq` to run Nextflow workflows, NCI created the [persistent sessions]() nodes. These nodes do not have a walltime limit imposed, and are accessed via ssh rather than through the job scheduler. If running the Nextflow workflow in the foreground, your workflow will be killed as soon as the ssh connection to the persistent session is closed. To enable you to log off without killing the run, start a 'screen' or 'tmux' session within your persistent session. Start the workflow with the Nextflow `run` command from within your screen/tmux session, then detach from the screen once your workflow is running. You can reconnect to the persistent session then reattach to your screen/tmux session at any time to check on your run.

### Monitoring your run

When running your workflow with a Gadi configuration file from the persistent sessions or `copyq`, you can monitor using the `qstat` command in the usual way. The `qstat` command will show job IDs for all Nextflow processes that have been submitted. When using `copyq`, you will also see the status of the head job. If you observe that the walltime is running low but the workflow is not near completion, please contact the NCI helpdesk to increase the walltime of the Nextflow head job on `copyq`. 


### Use of login nodes

Gadi's login nodes are *not* intended for running Nextflow workflows. However, they can be used to help set up your run, for example, pulling the workflow and dependencies or running very small tests (for example, the ubiquitous '[hello world](https://training.nextflow.io/latest/hello_nextflow/01_hello_world/#1-examine-the-script-and-run-it)' learning activity). 

The login nodes are throttled, so if you start a Nextflow workflow on the login node, it will be aborted if any of the walltime, CPU or memory resource caps applied to the login nodes are met. Even if you are using a Nextflow Gadi config to send processes to the PBS Pro job scheduler, the Nextflow head job must stay active for the duration of these running processes. Since commands are killed after 30 minutes on the login node, this method will fail for most non-trivial workflow runs.

Many public Nextflow workflows include test datasets. In some cases, the test datasets can run successfully on the login node, and can be a good way to ensure you have all the workflow requirements locally before running on the network-inaccessible compute nodes. Some test datasets exceed the login node resource caps, so test runs may require to be submitted using the Gadi configuration described above. 

## Single PBS job for simple workflows

If your workflow is simple, you can run the workflow within a single PBS job on any of the compute queues without a configuration file. Simply include the `nextflow run` command under your PBS directives as normal. 

Running complex workflow on Gadi in this way is not ideal as it restricts Nextflow to using only the 'local resources', ie only those that are contained on that single node. Consider the example of a workflow where there are 100 samples each moving through a process requiring 12 CPU and 24 GB on the `normal` queue. A job which requests one whole `normal` node (i.e. 48 CPU and 190 GB RAM) to run this workflow could only run at most 4 of these 100 processes at a time. If the same workflow was executed with a Gadi configuration file, all 100 runs of that process would be submitted as separate jobs, increasing throughput and reducing user wait time. 

Similarly, if some processes in the workflow required GPU or huge memory, this could not be achieved with this example job. Those processes would be forced to run on the same node that the Nextflow head job was running on, likely leading to reduced performance or job failure. 

An example simple Nextflow run script for the `normal` queue is shown below: 

```bash
#!/bin/bash

#PBS -P <nci-project-code>
#PBS -q normal
#PBS -l ncpus=48
#PBS -l mem=190GB
#PBS -l jobfs=200GB
#PBS -l walltime=48:00:00
#PBS -l gdata/<nci-project-code>
#PBS -l wd

module load nextflow/<version>
module load singularty

nextflow run <path-to-my>/main.nf -with-singularity --<parameter1> <argument1> --<parameter2> <argument2> 

```
## Example Gadi configuration files

### nf-core Gadi config

Nexflow workflows from the nf-core repository are very popular. If you haven't used nf-core before, we recommend you check it out to see if there is a workflow to suit your needs. The nf-core team have prepared a Gadi config to work with their standardised workflow format. The Gadi config can be found [here](https://nf-co.re/configs/nci_gadi/). 

### Custom workflow Gadi config

We have prepared two template configs that can be used for custom (non nf-core) Nextflow workflows. The Gadi environment configurations are separated from the module (process) configurations. The environment config can run any* custom Nextflow workflow on Gadi, where the modules config should be able to run the workflow on any other HPC, along with its appropriately set up environment config. This separation makes portability easier.  

*** *To work with any Nextflow workflow, the workflow must include the parameters `storage_account`, `su_account`, and `outdir`.***: 

- `storage_account`: Comma delimited list of all projects with input or output filepaths required for the run. The user's default NCI project need not be listed as both `scratch` and `gdata` are loaded for the user's default project. For example, `--storage_account ab12,cd34` will load scratch and gdata for the user's default NCI project AND projects ab12 and cd34.
- `su_account`: KSU will be charged from the user's default project, unless over-ridden by this command-line parameter, for example `--su_account cd34`.
- `outdir`: Specifies the name of the output directory.


#### Environment config

Note that the environment config shown below does not need to be edited with any user names, project codes, process names, or resource details. Its function is to get Nextflow running on Gadi for the submitting user. Note also that singularity is specified for software, which is preferred on Gadi. 

```groovy,title="gadi.environment.config"
// NCI has a specialised patched install of Nextflow. See: https://opus.nci.org.au/display/DAE/Nextflow
// this allows for things like storage (PBS -l storage) 


//----------PARAMS----------//
params { 
    whoami = System.getenv('USER') ?: System.getenv('LOGNAME')
    su_account = System.getenv("PROJECT")
    storage_account = '' // list all on CLI, eg --storage_account ab12,cd34
    storage = null // will hold default (su_account scratch and gdata) plus scratch and gdata for all projects provided to --storage_account
    singularityCacheDir = ''
}


//----------SINGULARITY----------// 
singularity {
    enabled = true
    autoMounts = true
    autoCleanUp = true
    cacheDir = params.singularityCacheDir ? params.singularityCacheDir
        : "/scratch/${params.su_account}/${params.whoami}/.nextflow/singularity"	
}


//----------STORAGE----------//
// Enable provision of multiple storage paths for '-l storage' directive - create at top level
// collect all scratch and gdata paths if provided with --storage_account optional parameter 
ext.storageAccountString = { s ->
    (s ?: '')
    .split(',')
    .collect { it.trim() }
    .findAll { it }
    .unique()
    .collect { p -> "scratch/${p}+gdata/${p}" }
    .join('+')
}


// Build the final storage string into params.storage (global scope)
params.storage = (params.storage && params.storage.trim()) ? params.storage
    : "scratch/${params.su_account}+gdata/${params.su_account}" +
    (params.storage_account ? "+${ext.storageAccountString(params.storage_account)}" : "")


//----------EXECUTOR----------// 
// stable PBS polling, global job query (not by queue) = true
// recommended: false
executor {
    queueGlobalStatus = false 
    pollInterval      = '2 min'
    queueStatInterval = '10 min'
    
    retry {
        maxAttempt = 5
        delay      = '10 sec'
        maxDelay   = '30 sec'
        jitter     = 0.25
        reason     = '.*(cannot connect to server|Connection timed out|Socket timed out).*'
    }    
    
}


//----------RUNINFO----------//
// Define timestamp, to avoid overwriting existing trace
def timestamp = new java.util.Date().format('yyyy-MM-dd_HH-mm-ss')

// Produce a workflow diagram
dag {
    enabled = true
    file = "${params.outdir}/run_info/dag_${timestamp}.svg"
}

report {
    enabled = true
    file = "${params.outdir}/run_info/report_${timestamp}.html"
}

timeline {
    enabled = true
    file = "${params.outdir}/run_info/timeline_${timestamp}.html"
}

trace {
    enabled = true
    file = "${params.outdir}/run_info/trace_${timestamp}.txt"
    fields = 'process,name,status,queue,realtime,cpus,%cpu,memory,%mem,rss,env'
} 



//----------PROCESS----------// 
process {
    // Fail a task if any command returns non-zero exit code
    shell = ['/bin/bash', '-euo', 'pipefail']

    //General
    module = 'singularity'
    cache = 'lenient'
    executor = 'pbspro'

    // Gadi accounting
    project = "${params.su_account}"
    storage = params.storage   // NCI-patched Nextflow maps this to PBS -l storage - otherwise, add to clusterOptions
} 

```

#### Workflow config 

Unlike the environment config above which is workflow-agnostic, this config is specific to the workflow. Adjust the example process names and resourcing to match your specific Nextflow workflow. 

Note that local execution (the resources used by the head node, eg `copyq` or persistent session) and 1 CPU and 4 GB RAM is assigned by default for all processes not covered by `withName` or `withLabel`. 

The template config makes use of process labels to group processes that require similar resources. This makes adapting the template to a new workflow simpler, by reducing the need to set `withName` for each of the numerous processes in your workflows. For example to request 7 CPU, 63 GB RAM, and 7 hours for a process on the `normalbw` nodes, add the line of code `label 'moderate_high_mem'` to your process code.

An example `withName` resourcing block is included for CPU and GPU processes that don't match the geenral requirements covered byt he resource labels. You can have as many `withName` resource blocks as you like within your config, but longer configs require greater maintenance effort!

As always, when determining your workflow resources, benchmarking is highly recommended. The workflow used when developing these template configs benchmarked best to `gpuhopper` queue, but this may not be the case for your GPU process! 

```groovy,title="gadi.environment.config"
// Set default resources for each process
process {
    // Set default resources for all processes
    cpus = 1
    memory = 4.GB
    executor = 'local'
    
    withName: 'CUSTOM_CPU_PROCESS' {
        // -29 specific exitcode for gadi exceeded walltime gives rise to 143 exitcode seen by nextflow
        // some samples require extreme walltimes compared to most others
        errorStrategy = { task.exitStatus == 143 ? 'retry' : 'terminate' }
        time = {4.h * task.attempt}
        cpus = 12
        memory = 48.GB
        queue = 'normal'
        maxRetries = 3    
    }	

    withName: 'CUSTOM_GPU_PROCESS' {
        time = 24.h
        cpus = 24
        memory = 512.GB
        maxForks = 50 // max jobs per user on DGX queue
        queue = 'gpuhopper'
        // cpu and mem ignored with clusterOptions -l, and no gpus param so must add all to clusterOptions - will emit warning
        clusterOptions = { "-l ngpus=2,ncpus=${task.cpus},mem=${task.memory.toGiga()}GB,jobfs=200GB,storage=${params.storage}" }
        // For GPU jobs, Singularity must be run with --nv so CUDA libraries/devices are injected
        containerOptions = '--nv'
    }
		
    withLabel: 'moderate_high_mem' {
        time = 4.h
        cpus = 7
        memory = 63.GB
        queue = 'normalbw'    
    }	
    withLabel: 'single_core_high_mem' {
        time = 4.h
        cpus = 2
        memory = 63.GB
        queue = 'normalbw'    
    }		
 	    
    withLabel: 'light' {
        cpus = 4
        memory = 16.GB
        time = 30.m
        queue = 'normal'
    }   
    
    withLabel: 'moderate' {
        cpus = 12
        memory = 48.GB
        time = 1.h
        queue = 'normal'
    }
    
    withLabel: 'large_fast' {
        cpus = 24
        memory = 96.GB
        time = 10.m
        queue = 'normal'
    }
    
    withLabel: 'large' {
        cpus = 24
        memory = 96.GB
        time = 6.h
        queue = 'normal'
    }    
           
    withLabel: 'large_slow' {
        cpus = 24
        memory = 96.GB
        time = 12.h
        queue = 'normal'
    }    
    
    withLabel: 'high_mem' {
        cpus        = 12
        memory      = { 48.GB * task.attempt }
        time        = { 4.h * task.attempt }
        queue       = 'normal'
        errorStrategy = 'retry'
        maxRetries  = 1  
    }
}
```

#### Custom configurations syntax

To use these custom template configs in your run, ensure to include both in your run command, e.g.:

`nextflow run <workflow> <parameters> -c /path/to/gadi.environment.config -c /path/to/gadi.modules.config`

or 

`nextflow run <workflow> <parameters> -c /path/to/gadi.environment.config,/path/to/gadi.modules.config`

Alternatively, you can group multiple configurations into a [profile](https://sydney-informatics-hub.github.io/customising-nfcore-workshop-2026/session_2/2.2_config/#2242-using-a-custom-configuration-profile). 

## Run on the `copyq` with a Gadi configuration file

Shown below is an example script to run the Nextflow head job (`run` command) on the `copy` queue while sending individual processes to the PBS Pro scheduler to run across the cluster according to the Gadi config/s. The example below specifies 2 custom configurations as described in [Custom workflow Gadi config](#custom-workflow-gadi-config.) If you are running an nf-core workflow, please use `-profile singularity,nci_gadi` as described [here](https://nf-co.re/configs/nci_gadi/) instead of `-c /path/to/gadi.environment.config,/path/to/gadi.modules.config`

```bash
#!/bin/bash

#PBS -P <nci-project-code>
#PBS -q copyq
#PBS -l ncpus=1
#PBS -l mem=4GB
#PBS -l walltime=10:00:00
#PBS -l gdata/<nci-project-code>
#PBS -l wd

module load nextflow/<version>
module load singularty

nextflow run <workflow> --<parameter1> <argument1> --<parameter2> <argument2> -c /path/to/gadi.environment.config,/path/to/gadi.modules.config`

# For nf-core:
#nextflow run <workflow> --<parameter1> <argument1> --<parameter2> <argument2> -profile singularity,nci_gadi`
```

## Run on the persistent session nodes with a Gadi configuration file

1. Connect to a persistent session. Follow the [NCI guide to starting and connecting to a persistent session](https://opus.nci.org.au/spaces/Help/pages/241927941/Persistent+Sessions...). If you have previously started a session and forgot its name, you can recover a list of past session names by running `ls ~/.persistent-sessions/`.
2. Open a `tmux` or `screen` session. Commands for `screen` will be included here. Start a screen session: `screen -S <your-screen-name>`
3. Start your nextflow run. This may be by entering the full Nextflow command (e.g. `nextflow run <workflow> <parameters> -c /path/to/gadi.config`) or running a shell script with your saved Nextflow run command. Ensure to specify the Gadi config at the `-c` Nextflow parameter. 
4. Once your run has started, detach from the screen: `ctrl A + D`
5. Monitor your processes with `qstat` as desired/required
6. When you are ready to view the status of your run,  you can reconnect to the persistent session and then the `screen` session. This need not be from the same terminal session. Command: `screen -r <your-screen-name>`. If you have forgotten the name of your screen, you can list screen sessions with the command `screen -list`

If the Nextflow run has completed successfully, you will see the green summary details and have a command prompt. If it is still running, you will see the process status bar and have no command prompt. If the run has failed with error, you will see red error messages and have a command prompt. In the case of error, check the process error log as described in 'Debugging' below. 



## Debugging

If you need to debug an error from a Nextflow run making use of a Gadi config and PBS-scheduled processes, you will find the PBS Pro error log of individual processes within the `work` directory of that process. The work directory path will be printed to as an error message to the terminal when the run fails. 

The PBS Pro error log which we usually find at `<job-name>.e<job-id>` will for example look like `work/dc/5184fdc7c63198d41a03c73790b7f6/<process-name>.log`. 

It can also be useful to check the command that was run by the process, for example `work/dc/5184fdc7c63198d41a03c73790b7f6/command.sh`.

If you have run a single PBS job where all processes are running within the same block of resources (i.e. no Gadi configuration file) your standard PBS Pro `.e` error and `.o` log files can be checked as usual.
